title: When the PDF Started Oversharing: From XXE to Reading /etc/passwd
summary_en: A PDF export feature was found to be vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) injection, allowing an attacker to read sensitive server files like /etc/passwd by embedding them into the generated document.

lesson.cause: The root cause was an insecurely configured XML parser used by the /api/generate-pdf endpoint. XML (a format for organizing data) allows for 'Entities,' which are essentially variables. The server's parser was configured to allow 'External Entities,' which are instructions to fetch data from external sources or local files. Because the parser did not restrict these entities, it followed the researcher's instruction to read a system file and include its content in the XML structure, which was then rendered into the final PDF.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Locate the 'Export as PDF' feature within the application.
2. Click the button to trigger a document generation request.
DISCOVERY
3. Open Burp Suite (a tool used to intercept and modify web traffic) to monitor the request.
4. Identify the specific endpoint being used: POST /api/generate-pdf.
5. Observe the 'Content-Type: application/xml' header, indicating the server expects XML data.
6. Examine the XML body of the request:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><document><title>Security Report</title><author>Researcher</author><content>Report content goes here.</content></document>
Why: This shows the application takes user-controlled XML tags like <title> and <content> and puts them in the PDF.
TESTING
7. Formulate a hypothesis that the XML parser (software that reads XML) might be vulnerable to XXE (a bug where the parser follows malicious shortcuts).
8. Modify the request to include a DOCTYPE (a section that defines XML rules) with an external entity.
9. Use a payload designed to trigger an external interaction:
<!DOCTYPE test [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://[YOUR_COLLABORATOR_ID].oastify.com"> ]>
Why: The 'SYSTEM' keyword tells the server to fetch data from the provided URL (a beginner gloss: like telling the server to visit a website).
10. Reference the entity '&xxe;' inside one of the tags:
<content>&xxe;</content>
Why: The '&' and ';' tell the parser to replace this text with whatever the 'xxe' variable fetched.
11. Send the request and check Burp Collaborator (a tool that listens for server connections) for a DNS or HTTP hit.
12. Confirm the server attempted to reach the external URL, proving it processes external entities.
EXPLOITATION
13. Change the external entity to target a local file on the server instead of a URL.
14. Use the following payload to target the Linux password file:
<!DOCTYPE test [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]>
Why: The 'file://' protocol tells the server to look at its own internal storage (a beginner gloss: like opening a file on your own hard drive).
15. Ensure the entity reference '&xxe;' is still inside the <content> tag.
16. Send the finalized malicious request to the /api/generate-pdf endpoint.
IMPACT
17. Receive the generated PDF file from the server response.
18. Open the PDF and observe that the 'content' section now contains the text of the server's /etc/passwd file.
Why: The server read the file, put it into the XML, and then 'printed' that XML into the PDF document.
lesson.example: Suppose a fictional site 'target.example' has a 'Update Profile' feature that uses XML. A normal request looks like: <user><name>Alice</name><bio>Hello!</bio></user>. An attacker sends: <!DOCTYPE r [<!ENTITY shhh SYSTEM "file:///C:/Windows/win.ini">]><user><name>Alice</name><bio>&shhh;</bio></user>. If the server is vulnerable, Alice's profile 'bio' will now display the contents of the server's internal Windows configuration file. This works because the XML parser is not told to ignore 'SYSTEM' entities, so it fetches the file content and treats it as part of the user's bio text.
lesson.takeaway: Always test features that generate documents (PDF, Excel, Word) or accept structured data (XML, SVG, JSON). Use 'Out-of-Band' (OOB) testing with tools like Burp Collaborator to find 'blind' XXE where the server doesn't show you the result directly. A common variant is XXE via SVG file uploads, as SVGs are actually XML files. A common beginner mistake is assuming that if an app uses JSON, it isn't vulnerable; however, many servers will still process XML if you manually change the 'Content-Type' header to 'application/xml'.
lesson.fix: The most effective fix is to completely disable DTDs (Document Type Definitions) and external entity processing in the XML parser configuration. In Java, this is done by setting specific features on the DocumentBuilderFactory. For example: factory.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true); and factory.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false);. This ensures the parser ignores any 'SYSTEM' or 'ENTITY' instructions provided by the user.

title: One File, Zero Clicks Needed: A Stored DoS Story
summary_en: A researcher discovered that a diagramming tool's SVG upload feature was vulnerable to a 'Billion Laughs' XML expansion attack, allowing a low-privilege user to permanently crash diagrams for all collaborators.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by the server-side XML parser failing to disable entity expansion when processing SVG files. Since SVGs are XML-based, they support 'entities' (text shortcuts). The application's parser would dutifully attempt to expand these shortcuts even when they were nested exponentially, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) as the server exhausted its memory and CPU resources trying to resolve a tiny file into gigabytes of data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified a diagramming tool with a feature allowing users to upload custom shape libraries as SVG files.
(An SVG is an image format that uses XML text to define shapes).

DISCOVERY
2. The researcher noted that SVGs are essentially XML files, which are often susceptible to entity-based attacks.
(XML is a language used to store and transport data).
3. They decided to test for a 'Billion Laughs' attack, which uses nested shortcuts to overwhelm a computer.
(An entity is a shortcut in XML that represents a larger string of text).

EXPLOITATION
4. The researcher prepared a malicious SVG file containing the 'Billion Laughs' XML structure.
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
 <!ENTITY lol "lol">
 <!ENTITY lol1 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
 <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;">
]>
<svg>&lol2;</svg>
Why: This payload defines 'lol1' as ten 'lol's, and 'lol2' as ten 'lol1's. Each level multiplies the size by 10. A full version with 9 levels results in 1 billion 'lol's from a tiny file.
5. The researcher uploaded this SVG into the 'custom shape library' section of a diagram.
6. They dragged the malicious shape onto the active drawing canvas.
7. The application immediately became unresponsive, showing a permanent loading state.
Why: The server's parser (the software reading the file) got stuck in an infinite loop of expanding the shortcuts, consuming all available resources.

IMPACT
8. To confirm the 'Stored' nature of the bug, the researcher logged in as a different user (the high-privilege owner of the diagram).
9. The owner attempted to open the diagram that the collaborator had modified.
10. The owner's screen also hung indefinitely, effectively locking them out of their own work.
Why: Because the malicious SVG was saved as part of the diagram's state, the server tried to process it for every single user who viewed that diagram.
lesson.example:
Imagine a project management app at target.example where users can upload SVG icons for their tasks. An attacker uploads 'bomb.svg' containing nested entities. 

Attack Request:
POST /api/tasks/101/icon HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: image/svg+xml

<svg>
<!DOCTYPE bomb [
<!ENTITY a "RESOURCES">
<!ENTITY b "&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;&a;">
<!ENTITY c "&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;&b;">
]>
<rect width="100" height="100">&c;</rect>
</svg>

When any team member views the task list, their browser or the server (depending on where the SVG is processed) will attempt to expand '&c;' into 100 instances of 'RESOURCES'. If the attacker adds more levels (d, e, f...), the expansion reaches billions of characters, crashing the app for the entire team.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always treat SVG upload fields as XML entry points. Test for both XXE (reading files) and XML Entity Expansion (crashing the server). This 'Stored DoS' pattern is particularly valuable because it proves you can disrupt other users' workflows without their interaction. Look for any app that processes XML-based formats like SVG, DOCX, or XLSX. A common mistake is thinking that 'image' uploads are safe; if the file is text-based like an SVG, it is a potential logic bomb.
lesson.fix: The fix is to configure the XML parser to explicitly disable Document Type Definitions (DTDs) and external entity resolution. In most programming languages, this is done by setting specific security flags on the parser object. For example, in Java using the DocumentBuilderFactory, you should set 'setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true)'. This prevents the parser from even looking at the malicious entity definitions, neutralizing the attack before it starts.
